question: Middleware A calls next(), then Middleware B calls next(), then a route handler sends a response. What happens if Middleware A calls next() again after the handler completes?
options: next() triggers Middleware B again, creating an infinite loop
next() has no effect; calling it after the response is sent does nothing
Express throws an error 'Response already sent'
The response is sent twice, doubling the data
explanation: Calling next() after the response is sent is a no-op; Express doesn't error, but no further middleware runs because the response is complete.

question: A middleware logs req.method, then calls next(). Inside the next() callback, it tries to modify req.method = 'DELETE'. The route handler sees req.method as POST. Why?
options: next() doesn't return control to the middleware after the handler runs
Modifying req after the handler processes it has no effect on that handler
req.method is read-only and cannot be modified
Express creates a copy of req before the handler, so changes are lost
explanation: next() is not a callback function; it immediately passes control forward and doesn't return, so code after next() in the middleware won't run until the response is sent (if at all).

question: Error-handling middleware is defined as (err, req, res, next) => { ... }. It's registered after route handlers. A synchronous error is thrown in a route. Why doesn't the error handler catch it?
options: Synchronous errors are never caught by error middleware
Error middleware must be registered before route handlers to work
The error middleware must explicitly listen to thrown errors with process.on()
Synchronous errors in routes are auto-caught by Express only if async/await is used
explanation: Error-handling middleware must be registered after all other middleware and routes; if registered before routes, it won't catch route errors. Also, sync errors must be explicitly passed to next(err).

question: Middleware calls res.json({data: 'test'}), then res.send('more'). What happens?
options: Both methods send their data; the client receives both responses
res.send() throws an error because the response is already sent
Only res.json() sends; res.send() is silently ignored
res.send() overwrites the previous response
explanation: After res.json() sends the response, res.send() silently fails because the response is already sent; Express prevents double-sending with internal flags.

question: A middleware modifies req.headers.authorization and calls next(). The route handler logs req.headers.authorization. Will it see the modified value?
options: No; req.headers is read-only after the request enters Express
Yes; modifying req.headers affects the original object
Only if next() is awaited like await next()
Only if the modification is done before app.use() is called
explanation: req.headers is a mutable object; modifications in middleware persist through the request chain because they're on the same req object.

question: Middleware A takes 30s to complete before calling next(). Middleware B and the route handler then run. Meanwhile, another request arrives and goes through Middleware A again. Why don't they block each other?
options: Express queues requests and processes them sequentially
Each request has its own context; Middleware A's 30s timer is per-request, not shared
Node.js runs multiple threads, one per request
Express automatically skips slow middleware for new requests
explanation: Node.js is single-threaded but asynchronous; each request maintains its own stack, so waiting in Middleware A for the first request doesn't block the second's execution.

question: Custom middleware stores user data in req.user = {id: 123}. Later middleware tries req.user.name = 'John' but gets 'Cannot set property name of undefined'. Why?
options: req.user is read-only and cannot have properties added
The first middleware didn't assign req.user before the second middleware ran
req.user is set to null instead of an object
Each middleware gets a separate copy of req, so changes don't propagate
explanation: If the first middleware didn't execute or didn't set req.user, the second middleware sees req.user as undefined; ensure middleware runs in the correct order.

question: A middleware uses app.use(bodyParser.json({limit: '10kb'})). A POST request with a 5MB body is sent. Why does it fail?
options: The body is larger than the 10kb limit, so the parser rejects it
bodyParser silently ignores large bodies and req.body is undefined
Express rejects the request before it reaches middleware
The body is truncated to 10kb automatically
explanation: bodyParser enforces size limits; exceeding the limit raises a 413 Payload Too Large error and req.body is not set.

question: Middleware is registered as app.use('/api', middlewareFunc). A request to /users is processed. Does middlewareFunc run?
options: Yes; app.use() middleware runs for all routes regardless of path
No; the path prefix /api prevents the middleware from running for /users
Only if /users starts with /api
Yes, but only if a route is defined for /users
explanation: Middleware registered with a path prefix only runs for routes matching that prefix; /users doesn't start with /api, so middlewareFunc is skipped.

question: An async middleware is registered: app.use(async (req, res, next) => { await somePromise(); next(); }). An error is thrown inside somePromise(). Why doesn't the error handler catch it?
options: Async errors in middleware are always ignored by Express
The error is thrown but next() was already called before the promise rejected
Errors in async middleware must be caught with try-catch and passed to next(err)
Express doesn't support async/await syntax in middleware
explanation: Express doesn't automatically catch promise rejections; wrap async code in try-catch and call next(err) to trigger error-handling middleware.
